segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “There was a rich man who had a manager, and this manager was accused to him of squandering his property.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So he called him and said to him, ‘What is this I hear about you? Hand over the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, now that my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from the management people will welcome me into their homes.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And he summoned each one of his master’s debtors. He said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said, ‘A hundred measures of olive oil.’ The manager told him, ‘Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then he said to another, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He told him, ‘Take your bill and write eighty.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the master praised the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly; for the sons of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth, so that when it gives out they will welcome you into the eternal tents.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much, and whoever is dishonest in very little is dishonest also in much.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So if you have not been faithful with dishonest wealth, who will trust you with true wealth?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No household slave can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, were listening to all this, and they sneered at him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are the ones who justify yourselves before people, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among people is an abomination before God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is being proclaimed, and everyone is forcing their way into it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter in the Law to fall.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: There was a rich man who dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted in splendor every day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And a poor man named Lazarus had been laid at his gate, covered with sores

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and longing to eat his fill of what fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs would come and lick his sores.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The time came when the poor man died and was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am in agony in this flame.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you received your good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise the bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in agony.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who want to cross from here to you cannot, and no one may cross from there to us.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said, ‘Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house—

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for I have five brothers—to warn them, so that they too will not come to this place of torment.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said, ‘No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will turn back.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”

notes.note: The word names the agent who ran a wealthy man’s estate and could make binding contracts in his name. “Steward” is the traditional rendering, but it now suggests a ship or a wine waiter; most modern versions use “manager”. The related words in verses 2–4 are rendered “management” and “be manager” to keep the repetition.

The Greek names two different Hebrew units: the bath, a liquid measure, for the oil, and the cor, a dry measure, for the wheat in verse 7. Estimates of their size vary, but a hundred baths was several thousand liters of oil and a hundred cors was many tons of grain. These are large commercial debts, and the reductions are worth a great deal.

The Greek word can mean the manager’s master, as in verses 3 and 5, or “the Lord”, meaning Jesus. Most interpreters take it as the master inside the story, with Jesus’ own comment beginning at “for the sons of this age” or at verse 9. On the other reading the parable ends at verse 7 and this sentence is Luke’s report that Jesus praised the manager.

The word is a time-word: “this age” is the present era, contrasted in Jewish thought with the age to come. “Sons of” is a Semitic idiom for people who belong to something, here set against “sons of light”. Older versions have “world”; several modern versions already have “age”.

The Greek borrows an Aramaic word for money or property; “mammon” is not the name of a god, though Jesus speaks of it in verse 13 as a rival master. The phrase is literally “wealth of unrighteousness”, using the same word that describes the manager in verse 8. It may mean wealth gained dishonestly, but many scholars take it as wealth that belongs to this unjust age, hence “worldly wealth” in some versions.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and most versions generalize it here to “dwellings” or “homes”. The plain image is kept because it is striking: a tent is temporary, yet these belong to the age to come and last. “They” who do the welcoming may be the friends made by generosity, or it may be a reverent way of saying that God will welcome.

The word means a slave belonging to a household, and the verb rendered “serve” is the one for serving as a slave. Since a slave was owned outright, belonging to two masters is impossible in a way that working two jobs is not. Most versions have “servant”, and some have “slave”.

notes.phrase: everyone is forcing their way into it
notes.traditional: every man presseth into it / everyone forces his way into it
notes.note: The verb can be read as active in sense, as here, or as passive: “everyone is urgently pressed to enter it”. Both readings have scholarly support, and the similar saying in Matthew 11:12 is disputed in the same way. On either reading the point is that John’s arrival marks a new stage in which the kingdom is being announced.

The word means the chest or lap, or the fold of a garment over it. To be at someone’s chest was to recline next to them at a banquet, the place of honor and closeness, as in John 13:23. The beggar who longed for table scraps is given the best seat beside Abraham; “side” is the usual modern rendering of this image.

“Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which here would mean the brothers changing how they live. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

candidates.reason: Occurs here and in Matthew 6:24; translators divide among “mammon”, “wealth” and “money”, and the parallel sayings should match.
Recurs in Luke 12, 1 Corinthians 4, Titus 1 and 1 Peter 4, where “steward” and “manager” compete, and the cognates οἰκονομία and οἰκονομέω need to align with it.
Rendered variously “wise”, “sensible”, “prudent” and “shrewd” across the Gospels and Paul (Matthew 7:24, 10:16, 25:2; Luke 12:42), which hides that it is one word for practical good sense.
“Bosom”, “side”, “lap” and “heart” all appear in English versions for Luke 6:38, John 1:18, John 13:23 and here; the banquet-closeness image should be handled consistently.
The Semitic idiom “sons of X” for people belonging to something recurs widely (sons of the kingdom, of the resurrection, of disobedience), and versions vary among “sons”, “children” and “people”.
